cards.title: Logs — The Oldest Pillar
cards.teaser: A log is a time-stamped record of a discrete event. Every programming language, every operating system, and every runtime has been producing them for decades — logs are the original observability primitive.

runs.text: A log entry represents a single thing that happened at a specific point in time: a request arrived, a payment failed, a connection timed out, a configuration was reloaded. Unlike metrics (which aggregate over time) or traces (which follow a request across services), a log is a point event — it says "this happened, here, at this moment."
Logs are the oldest pillar of observability because they require almost no upfront design. Every
printf
statement, every
console.log
, every
System.out.println

is a log. The cost of entry is near zero. The result is that nearly every production system already has logs — but most of those logs were written to be read by a single developer in the moment of writing, not by a distributed log aggregation system under pressure at 2 AM.
A log entry has a minimum viable structure:

items.text: Timestamp
— when did this event occur? Always in UTC. Never local time.
Severity
— how important is this event? (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL)
Message
— a human-readable description of what happened.
Context
— structured fields that make the event searchable: request_id, user_id, service name, host, etc.

runs.text: The weakness of logs is volume and cost. A busy microservice can emit millions of log lines per hour. Storing, indexing, and querying that volume is expensive — Datadog, Splunk, and Elastic can consume a meaningful fraction of a company's infrastructure budget. This cost pressure is one reason the observability community has advocated for complementing logs with metrics (cheap, low-cardinality aggregations) and traces (sampling-friendly request graphs).

The verb "logging" predates software: ship captains kept a ship's log — a time-ordered record of events — from at least the 17th century. The CS usage is the same concept. An application log is exactly this: a time-ordered record of what happened aboard the system.
A log is a time-stamped record that says "this specific thing happened at this exact moment." It is the simplest form of observability — just write down what occurred as it occurs.

cards.title: Structured Logging — JSON vs printf
cards.teaser: Structured logging replaces free-form text with key-value pairs or JSON objects. The difference between printf-style and structured logs is the difference between logs humans read and logs machines can query.

runs.text: Printf-style logging looks like this:
2024-03-15T14:22:01Z ERROR Failed to process order 8821 for user 4409: timeout after 3000ms

This is readable to a human who can skim it. It is nearly unqueryable at scale. To find all timeout errors for user 4409, you need a regex. To compute average timeout durations, you need to parse free-form text. To join this log entry with a metric or trace, there is no machine-readable key to join on.
Structured logging emits the same event as a JSON object:
{"timestamp":"2024-03-15T14:22:01Z","level":"ERROR","event":"order_processing_failed","order_id":8821,"user_id":4409,"reason":"timeout","timeout_ms":3000,"service":"order-svc","trace_id":"abc123"}
Now the log entry is a first-class data record. A log aggregation system can:

items.text: Filter on exact field values:
user_id = 4409 AND reason = timeout
Compute aggregations: average
timeout_ms
per service over the last hour
Join with traces: look up the full distributed trace using
trace_id
Build dashboards from log data without writing parsing code

runs.text: The practical transition from printf to structured logging in most languages is one dependency change: replace
console.log
print()
with a structured logger (Python:
structlog
; Go:
slog
or
zap
; Java:
logback
with JSON encoder; Node:
pino
) and configure it to emit JSON to stdout. The log aggregation system picks up from there.

Do not log PII (names, emails, addresses, payment data) in structured fields — they become searchable and persistently stored. Design which fields are safe to index before instrumenting. What you log becomes your data retention problem.

Printf-style logs are sentences a human reads; structured logs are records a machine queries. The same event, but one lets you build dashboards and alerts while the other requires regex parsing at 2 AM.

cards.title: Log Levels — When to Use Each
cards.teaser: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, and FATAL are not aesthetic choices — each level is a contract about what triggered the log, who needs to see it, and what action (if any) is required.

runs.text: Log levels exist so that operators can filter signal from noise. In production, running at DEBUG verbosity would produce terabytes of data per hour and bury every real problem. The level system lets you dial verbosity per environment while keeping the same code paths.

items.text: DEBUG

— detailed internal state useful only to the developer actively debugging. Method entry/exit, variable dumps, SQL queries. Disabled in production by default. Never leave fine-grained DEBUG logs on in production; the volume cost is severe.
INFO

— normal operational events that confirm the system is working as expected. Request received, service started, configuration loaded, scheduled job completed. An operator watching the INFO stream should see a healthy system as a normal flow of events with no surprises.
WARN

— something unexpected happened but the system recovered or degraded gracefully. A retry succeeded, a fallback was used, a deprecated API was called, a threshold was approached but not exceeded. WARN means "pay attention, this might matter soon."
ERROR

— a specific operation failed in a way that requires attention. A request could not be fulfilled, a database write failed, an external API returned an unexpected error. Every ERROR should have an associated alert or at minimum be tracked in an error dashboard. If ERRORs are not actionable, they are noise — demote them to WARN.
FATAL

— the process is about to crash or must be terminated. Configuration is so broken the service cannot function, a required resource is irrecoverably unavailable. FATAL is logged once, then the process exits. Use sparingly — most error conditions are ERRORs, not fatals.

runs.text: A practical rule: in production, set the log level to INFO. Set it to DEBUG only on specific instances during active investigation and revert it immediately after. Never run FATAL or ERROR counts at zero in a healthy system — it means either the system never errors (unlikely) or errors are being silently swallowed.

Alarm fatigue is an observability anti-pattern caused by over-alerting on WARN and ERROR events that are expected or unactionable. If your on-call rotation sees hundreds of ERROR log alerts per hour and ignores most of them, the level system has been miscalibrated. Audit log levels the way you audit tests — each one should have a clear meaning and a clear owner.

Log levels are a filtering contract: DEBUG is for the developer's eyes only, INFO is "everything is normal," WARN is "something odd happened but we recovered," ERROR is "something broke and someone should look," and FATAL is "we're going down."

cards.title: Log Aggregation — Centralizing the Stream
cards.teaser: A microservices system might run hundreds of instances across dozens of services. Log aggregation is the practice of collecting all those streams into a single queryable store — without it, debugging means SSH-ing into individual machines and grepping.

runs.text: In a single-process application on a single server, logs are wherever the process writes them — a file, stdout. Debugging means
ssh app-server-1
and
tail -f /var/log/app.log
. This approach collapses when the application spans 40 services, each running 10 instances, scheduled across 200 Kubernetes pods that are replaced on every deploy.
Log aggregation centralizes logs from all sources into a single queryable system. The canonical pattern:

items.text: Collection
— an agent runs alongside each service and ships logs to the aggregation backend. Common agents: Fluentd, Fluent Bit, Vector, Filebeat. They read from stdout/files and forward to the backend.
Ingestion and indexing

— the backend parses, enriches, and indexes the log data. Common backends: Elasticsearch (the E in ELK/EFK stack), Loki (Grafana's label-based log storage), Splunk, Datadog Logs, Google Cloud Logging.
Query and visualization
— operators search across all services and time ranges with a query interface. Kibana (for Elasticsearch), Grafana (for Loki), Splunk Search, and Datadog Log Explorer are typical.

runs.text: A key design decision is
indexing vs. log lines

. Elasticsearch indexes every field — fast queries, high cost. Loki indexes only labels (service, environment, level) and treats the log body as unindexed text — lower cost, regex-based body search. Choose based on your query patterns and budget.
Correlation is the payoff of aggregation. When every log entry carries a
trace_id
or
request_id
, you can query for all log lines across all services for a single user request — a feat impossible without aggregation and structured logging working together.

Retention policy is the most frequently neglected aggregation design decision. Storing 30 days of logs for 100 services at INFO verbosity can cost tens of thousands of dollars per month. Design log volumes, sampling policies, and retention windows before a bill arrives.
Log aggregation means all your services ship their logs to one place, so instead of SSH-ing into 50 machines to find an error, you run one query that searches everything at once.

cards.title: Metrics — Numeric Measurements Over Time
cards.teaser: A metric is a named numeric measurement collected at regular intervals. Where logs capture discrete events, metrics capture the ongoing state of a system — request rate, error rate, CPU usage, queue depth — cheaply enough to store forever.

runs.text: The key properties that distinguish metrics from logs:

items.text: Fixed schema.
A metric is a name, a value, a timestamp, and a set of labels (key-value pairs). No free-form text. The schema is defined at instrumentation time.
Low cardinality.

Metrics aggregate events into counts or measurements. "5,000 requests in the last minute" is one data point; 5,000 log lines is 5,000 data points. This is why metrics cost orders of magnitude less than logs.
Time-series orientation.
Metrics are stored in time-series databases (Prometheus, InfluxDB, VictoriaMetrics, Datadog) optimized for range queries: "show me this metric over the last 24 hours."
Alertability.
Metrics are the natural substrate for alerting. "Alert when error rate exceeds 5% for 5 minutes" is a metric-based alert. Log-based alerts exist but are more expensive and slower.

runs.text: The standard model is the Prometheus data model, which has become the de facto standard for metrics instrumentation. A Prometheus metric looks like:
http_requests_total{method="POST",status="200",service="order-svc"} 15234
The name (
http_requests_total

), the labels (dimensions for slicing), and the value (15234) form a time series. Prometheus scrapes this endpoint on a configurable interval and stores the series over time. PromQL then lets you query it:
rate(http_requests_total[5m])
gives you requests per second over the last 5 minutes.
The four metric types — counter, gauge, histogram, and summary — define how the numeric value is collected and interpreted. Each serves a different measurement problem.

A metric is a number with a name and a timestamp, collected repeatedly over time. It answers "how much?" and "how fast?" at low cost — where logs say what happened, metrics say how the system is doing overall.

cards.title: Counter — Monotonic and Always Increasing
cards.teaser: A counter counts things that happen and never goes backward. Requests served, bytes written, errors thrown, jobs completed — anything you can count since the process started.

runs.text: A counter is the simplest metric type: a monotonically increasing integer (or float). It starts at zero when the process starts. It increments on each event. It never decrements. If the process restarts, it resets to zero — and monitoring systems are designed to handle this reset gracefully.
In Prometheus, a counter exposes a
_total
suffix by convention:
http_requests_total{status="500"} 482
The raw counter value (482 errors since last restart) is rarely interesting. What you actually want is the rate of change — how fast is this counter increasing right now?
PromQL:
rate(http_requests_total{status="500"}[5m])
— errors per second averaged over the last 5 minutes.
The
rate()

function divides the counter delta by the time window, handling resets automatically. This is why counters never decrement: if you see the counter drop, it is a process restart (reset to zero), not an undo of previous events.
rate()
detects and corrects for this.

items.text: Good counter use cases:
total HTTP requests, total errors by type, bytes received/sent, database queries executed, cache hits/misses, retries attempted.
Bad counter use cases:
current queue depth, active connections, memory usage, CPU utilization — anything that legitimately goes up and down. Use a gauge for those.

runs.text: The RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) for microservice health is built entirely on counters. Rate = rate(requests_total), Errors = rate(errors_total) / rate(requests_total), Duration = histogram quantiles. Counters are the backbone of the most commonly applied observability methodology.
A counter counts things that happen and can only go up — like an odometer. You rarely care about the raw total; you care about how fast it is increasing right now, which is what rate() gives you.

cards.title: Gauge — Point-in-Time Value
cards.teaser: A gauge represents the current value of something that can go up or down: temperature, queue depth, active connections, memory usage. Unlike a counter, a gauge's raw value is meaningful right now.

runs.text: A gauge is a metric that can arbitrarily increase or decrease. It represents the current state of a measured quantity at the moment of collection. There is no "rate of gauge" — you read the gauge value directly.
Examples in Prometheus format:

go_goroutines 142
process_resident_memory_bytes 52428800
http_active_connections{service="api"} 37
jobs_in_queue{queue="email"} 1204

Each of these values is meaningful at the moment it is read. The goroutine count might be 142 now and 89 in 30 seconds. The queue depth might spike to 5000 during a traffic burst and drain back to zero. These measurements track the current state of the system, not a cumulative count of events.
Common gauge use cases:

items.text: Resource utilization:
CPU%, memory bytes, disk bytes free
Concurrency:
active requests, open connections, goroutines/threads in flight
Queue depth:
messages waiting to be processed — a critical capacity signal
Configuration values:
current feature flag state, pool size, replica count
Temperatures and external readings:
anything from hardware sensors or external systems

runs.text: A common mistake is modeling an event count as a gauge (setting it to a value rather than incrementing). If you set
total_requests = 5000

you are using a gauge where a counter belongs. Counters survive process restarts gracefully because monitoring systems detect the reset; a gauge that resets to zero on restart appears as a sudden drop, not a process restart.
A gauge is like a thermometer — it tells you what the value is right now, and that current value is what you care about. It can go up or down freely, unlike a counter which can only go up.

cards.title: Histogram — Bucketed Distributions for Latency
cards.teaser: A histogram answers "how are values distributed?" — not just the average, but the shape: what fraction of requests complete in under 100ms, under 500ms, under 1s? Histograms are the correct tool for latency instrumentation.

runs.text: Averages hide tail latency. If your API averages 150ms but 1% of requests take 10 seconds, the average tells you nothing about the worst user experience. A histogram captures the full distribution by sorting observations into configurable buckets.
A Prometheus histogram exposes three time series for each metric:

http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1"} 8234
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.5"} 11023
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="1.0"} 11891
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="+Inf"} 12000
http_request_duration_seconds_sum 3127.5
http_request_duration_seconds_count 12000
Reading this: of 12,000 requests, 8,234 completed within 100ms (

means "less than or equal to"), 11,023 within 500ms, 11,891 within 1 second. The remaining 109 requests took longer than 1 second. The sum (3127.5 seconds) divided by the count (12,000) gives average latency (0.26s).
To compute a percentile (e.g., p99) from a histogram in PromQL:
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
This is an
approximation

— the true p99 may fall anywhere within the p99 bucket. The accuracy depends on bucket boundaries being well-chosen for your latency distribution. For a service where most requests are 10–100ms, default Prometheus buckets (0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10 seconds) are usually reasonable, but custom buckets improve precision.

Histograms are stored server-side (at the monitoring backend). Multiple histogram series can be aggregated across service instances — you can compute the p99 for all instances of a service combined, not just per-instance. This is their key advantage over summaries.

Prometheus Native Histograms (introduced in Prometheus 2.40) use a sparse bucket representation with automatic high-resolution bucketing, eliminating the need to pre-configure bucket boundaries. They are the recommended approach for new instrumentation when using a recent Prometheus version.

A histogram sorts each observation into a pre-defined bucket — like sorting balls by size. From those buckets you can compute approximate percentiles: p50, p95, p99. The trade-off is pre-defined boundaries and approximate (not exact) percentiles.

cards.title: Summary — Pre-Calculated Percentiles
cards.teaser: A summary calculates percentiles at the client side — in the application process — and exposes them as gauge-like values. The trade-off: exact percentiles at the cost of being unable to aggregate across instances.

runs.text: A summary is Prometheus's alternative to the histogram for latency measurement. Instead of sorting observations into configurable buckets and computing approximate percentiles server-side, a summary uses a sliding window algorithm (typically t-digest or HDR Histogram) to compute exact percentiles inside the application process.
A Prometheus summary exposes:

rpc_duration_seconds{quantile="0.5"} 0.047
rpc_duration_seconds{quantile="0.9"} 0.112
rpc_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"} 0.891
rpc_duration_seconds_sum 8942.7
rpc_duration_seconds_count 94210
The p50 (median) is exactly 47ms, the p99 is exactly 891ms. No bucket boundary approximation. The percentiles are calculated over a sliding time window (commonly the last 10 minutes) and the
quantile
labels are configured at instrumentation time.
The critical limitation: summary quantile series
cannot be aggregated

. If you have 10 replicas of a service, each exposing a p99, you cannot average those p99 values to get the fleet-wide p99 — that is mathematically incorrect. The "average of p99s" is not the p99 of the combined distribution.
Comparison between histogram and summary:

items.text: Histogram:
approximate percentiles, server-side calculation, aggregatable across instances, requires pre-configured buckets. Use when you have multiple instances and need fleet-wide percentiles.
Summary:
exact percentiles, client-side calculation, not aggregatable, no bucket configuration needed. Use for single-instance services or when exact per-instance percentiles are required.

runs.text: The Prometheus documentation explicitly recommends histograms over summaries for most use cases in distributed systems because histograms are aggregatable. If you are running more than one replica of any service, default to histograms unless you have a specific reason for exact per-instance percentile accuracy.

A summary computes exact percentiles inside the app process, while a histogram computes approximate ones on the server. The catch: summaries from multiple instances cannot be combined — you cannot average two p99s and get a valid p99.

cards.title: Traces — Request-Scoped Causality Across Services
cards.teaser: A trace is the complete story of a single request as it travels through a distributed system — which services it touched, in what order, how long each step took, and where it failed.

runs.text: Logs tell you what happened in each service. Metrics tell you how each service is performing in aggregate. But neither answers: "For this specific request that user 4409 made at 14:22 that returned a 500, which service caused the failure and why?"
Distributed tracing answers this. A trace is a directed acyclic graph of
spans

, each representing one unit of work. The graph captures the causal structure: "API gateway called auth service, auth service called user-db, API gateway called order service, order service called inventory service." The full tree of calls, with timing, is one trace.
The key properties of the tracing model:

items.text: Request-scoped.
One trace = one request (HTTP request, gRPC call, async job). Traces are never aggregated across requests — that is what metrics are for.
Causal, not temporal.
Spans in a trace are linked by parent-child relationships ("span B was caused by span A"), not just by happening in the same time window.
Sampling-friendly.

Storing every trace for every request at scale is prohibitively expensive. Most tracing systems sample — collecting 1% of traces (or 100% of error traces) and discarding the rest. Unlike logs and metrics, traces are designed with sampling as a first-class concern.

runs.text: The OpenTelemetry project (CNCF, the successor to OpenTracing and OpenCensus) is now the standard instrumentation layer for distributed tracing. OpenTelemetry SDKs (Go, Java, Python, JS, .NET, Ruby) instrument code once and export to any compatible backend: Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog, Lightstep.

A trace follows one specific request through every service it touches — like a GPS trail of that request's journey. It shows which service called which, how long each step took, and where something went wrong.

cards.title: Span — The Atom of a Trace
cards.teaser: A span represents a single named operation within a trace — a database query, an HTTP call, a cache lookup. Every span has a start time, a duration, a status, and attributes. Spans are linked to form the causal tree.

runs.text: If a trace is the full story of a request, a span is one sentence of that story. The OpenTelemetry specification defines the span data model precisely.
An OpenTelemetry span in JSON form (simplified):
Key fields:

items.text: traceId
— identifies which trace this span belongs to. All spans in one request share the same traceId.
spanId
— unique identifier for this specific span.
parentSpanId
— the spanId of the calling span. Absent on the root span. This is the linkage that forms the tree.
name
— a human-readable description of the operation. Low-cardinality: use "GET /api/orders/{id}" not "GET /api/orders/8821" — parameterize dynamic values.
kind
— SERVER (handling an inbound call), CLIENT (making an outbound call), INTERNAL (local operation), PRODUCER/CONSUMER (messaging).
attributes
— key-value pairs with metadata. OpenTelemetry semantic conventions define standard attribute names (http.method, db.system, rpc.service) for interoperability.
events
— time-stamped annotations within the span (cache miss, retry, error detail). A lightweight log-within-a-trace.

runs.text: Duration =
endTimeUnixNano - startTimeUnixNano

= 183ms for this span. A trace viewer (Jaeger, Zipkin, Grafana Tempo) displays spans as a Gantt chart, making it instantly visible which spans were sequential and which were parallel, and where the time was spent.
A span is one operation in a request's journey: it has a name, a start time, a duration, and a pointer to its parent. String spans together by their parent pointers and you get the full trace tree.

cards.title: Trace Context — Propagating Identity Across Services
cards.teaser: Trace context is how a distributed trace stays connected as a request crosses service boundaries. The TraceId and SpanId are injected into outbound calls as HTTP headers, so every service receiving the request can attach its spans to the correct trace.

runs.text: The fundamental challenge of distributed tracing is correlation: how does service B know that the HTTP request it received is part of the same trace as what service A started? The answer is trace context propagation — the active trace context is serialized into the request itself.
The W3C Trace Context specification (an official W3C recommendation since 2021) defines two HTTP headers:

traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
tracestate: rojo=00f067aa0ba902b7,congo=t61rcWkgMzE
The
traceparent
header encodes four fields: version (00), traceId (32 hex chars), parentSpanId (16 hex chars), and flags (01 = sampled). Service B reads this header and:

items.text: Extracts the traceId (uses the same traceId for all spans it creates within this request)
Sets the parentSpanId of its root span to the spanId from the incoming header
Creates its own spanId for its own work, and propagates both when making further downstream calls

runs.text: This cascades through the entire call graph. Every service in the chain reads the context, creates child spans, and passes the context forward. The result: all spans across all services share the same traceId and are linked by parent-child spanId references into a single coherent tree.

OpenTelemetry SDKs handle propagation automatically for common frameworks (Express.js, Spring, Django, gRPC). Manual propagation is needed for custom protocols, async queues, and message buses — in those cases you serialize the context into message headers (e.g., Kafka headers) instead of HTTP headers.

Sampling decisions are also carried in the trace context flags. When service A decides to sample a trace (set flags = 01), service B must respect that decision and record its spans. When A decides not to sample (flags = 00), B must also not record. Consistent sampling across the call graph is required for a coherent trace.

Trace context is the address label that every service stamps on its outbound calls — "this work belongs to trace ABC, and I am span XYZ." The receiving service reads the label, attaches its spans to the same trace, then stamps the label on its own outbound calls.

cards.title: The Three-Pillars Critique — Observability Is One Thing
cards.teaser: "Logs, metrics, and traces" is a useful taxonomy for tooling — but framing them as three separate pillars obscures that observability is a single property: can you understand your system's internal state from its external outputs?

runs.text: The three-pillars model — sometimes attributed to Peter Bourgon's 2017 article "Metrics, tracing, and logging" — was an organizational framework for tool categories, not a definition of observability itself. It has been enormously useful for structuring tooling conversations. It has also created a problematic side effect: teams treat the pillars as checkboxes.
"We have Datadog for logs, Prometheus for metrics, and Jaeger for traces. We have all three pillars. We are observable."
Charity Majors, Liz Fong-Jones, and George Miranda argued in
Observability Engineering

(O'Reilly, 2022) that this framing misses the point. Observability is not three tools — it is a property of a system. A system is observable if operators can ask arbitrary questions about its internal state and get answers without deploying new code. The tools are means to that end, not the end itself.
The critique has four parts:

items.text: The pillars overlap.
Span events are logs. Metrics can be derived from traces. Structured log fields can feed metric aggregations. The boundaries between pillars are porous, not architectural.
The pillars are siloed in practice.

Most teams use different tools for each pillar with different query languages (PromQL for metrics, Lucene for logs, proprietary trace UIs). Debugging requires mental context-switching between three systems. Vendors like Honeycomb, Grafana, and Datadog have invested heavily in correlation — linking from a trace to its logs to the relevant metrics — precisely because siloed pillars break the investigation workflow.
High-cardinality context is the missing piece.

The pillar model encourages treating metrics as low-cardinality (no user IDs in metric labels) and traces as sampled. Majors et al. argue that wide structured events — single highly-contextual records that carry all relevant fields — enable queries that no combination of traditional logs, metrics, and traces can answer cheaply.
Observability requires active investment, not passive collection.
Having three tools does not make you observable if you cannot answer new questions about production without deploying code. The test is whether your team can debug novel failures.

runs.text: The three-pillar framework remains useful as a starting vocabulary and tooling guide. The critique is not that logs, metrics, and traces are wrong — it is that treating each pillar as a separate concern, owned by separate teams and stored in separate systems, produces observable-looking infrastructure that is not actually observable under pressure. The goal is answerable questions, not checkbox coverage.

Having logs, metrics, and traces does not make your system observable — it gives you the raw material. Observable means you can answer any question about what your system is doing right now without deploying new code. The pillars are a means to that end, not the end itself.
